questions.scenario: A retailer is kicking off a Claude feature that reads incoming supplier invoices and posts structured entries to its ERP. Stakeholders have agreed what the feature must do: extract vendor, amounts and line items, detect duplicates, and flag anything ambiguous for a human. The team now disagrees on infrastructure — one engineer wants to commit immediately to the largest model tier and the direct API "so we don't under-build."
questions.stem: According to requirements-driven design, what should the team do next before committing to an integration approach?

options.text: Provision the most capable model tier now, because downgrading after launch is easier than upgrading later.

Derive measurable non-functional requirements first — invoice volume, acceptable delay, data sensitivity, cost per invoice, accuracy floor — and let those drive the model tier, API mode, and platform.
Build a multi-agent pipeline with specialized extraction, validation, and routing subagents so the architecture can absorb any future requirement.
Start with the cheapest model and the simplest integration, then let production incidents reveal which requirements actually matter.

questions.explanation: Functional requirements (what the system does) are only half the input. The binding design inputs are the **non-functional requirements** — volume, acceptable delay, data sensitivity, cost per unit, accuracy floor — stated measurably so they can double as eval criteria and production monitors. Infrastructure choices (model tier, API mode, platform, controls) are then *derived* from those constraints; committing to them first inverts the process.

whyWrong.A: Picking the model tier before volume, latency tolerance, and cost per unit are quantified puts the cart before the horse; the tier should be selected to meet measured constraints, not pre-committed just in case.
whyWrong.C: A multi-agent pipeline multiplies cost, latency, and failure modes; complexity is justified only when requirements prove a single pass is insufficient, not as advance insurance.
whyWrong.D: Using production incidents as the requirements-discovery process pushes avoidable design risk onto real users when the business context already supplies the inputs needed to specify constraints.

questions.mindset: Infrastructure is derived from measurable requirements, never chosen first.

questions.scenario: During a design review for a new Claude-powered ticket-triage feature, the team cannot decide between the realtime Messages API and the Message Batches API. Both modes would produce identical output quality, but at materially different cost.
questions.stem: Which single question should the team answer first, because it most directly determines the right API mode?

options.text: How many tokens will the system prompt and few-shot examples consume per request?
Does the output need to be structured JSON or free-form text?
Who or what is waiting for each result, and how long can they wait?
Which programming language will the integration service be written in?

questions.explanation: "Who is waiting, and how long can they wait?" is the single most decisive question for Claude integrations: humans and blocking pipelines require realtime calls, while latency-tolerant bulk work can run through the Batches API at a substantial discount. Token counts, output format, and implementation language do not discriminate between the modes.

whyWrong.A: Token counts shape cost and context planning but do not distinguish realtime from batch — both modes process the same request body.
whyWrong.B: Structured output is available in both realtime and batch modes, so format does not select the mode.
whyWrong.D: Implementation language affects the codebase, not the latency tolerance that actually decides the integration mode.

questions.mindset: Who waits for the result decides realtime vs. batch.

questions.scenario: A platform team wants Claude to review every pull request for security anti-patterns before merge. The check runs in CI, the merge button stays blocked until a verdict posts to the PR, and developers start following up within a couple of minutes. A teammate proposes the Message Batches API to cut review cost roughly in half.
questions.stem: Which response best fits the stated requirements?

options.text: Submit reviews through the Message Batches API and poll the batch status every minute so verdicts post almost immediately.
Use the Batches API overnight when traffic is low and the realtime Messages API during working hours, behind the same code path.
Use the Batches API and let developers merge at their discretion once the review result eventually posts.
Keep the review on the realtime Messages API, because a blocked pipeline is latency-sensitive and batch results are only guaranteed within a 24-hour window.

questions.explanation: A merge gate is a blocking pipeline: a process waits on each individual result, which makes the workload latency-sensitive and rules out batches. Batch results arrive when the batch completes — most finish within an hour, but completion is only guaranteed within a 24-hour window, with no per-request SLA. Realtime calls (optionally streamed) fit the requirement.

whyWrong.A: Polling cannot make an asynchronous batch finish sooner; results arrive when the whole batch completes within the window, so the gate stays unpredictable.
whyWrong.B: A blocking merge gate is latency-sensitive regardless of the hour; maintaining two code paths still routes the reviews that matter through the wrong mode.
whyWrong.C: Letting developers merge before the verdict lands removes the gate the requirement defines; the check would no longer block anything.

questions.mindset: Blocking pipelines are latency-sensitive; batch windows are measured in hours.

questions.scenario: A product owner writes two requirements for a new customer-facing assistant: "The assistant must be accurate" and "It must feel fast to users." The engineers point out they cannot design, test, or monitor against either statement as written.
questions.stem: What is the best way to restate these requirements so they can drive design, evals, and production monitoring?

options.text: Restate them as measurable targets — a minimum quality score on an agreed benchmark set and a time-to-first-token threshold at peak load — and reuse those numbers as eval gates and live monitors.
Add system-prompt instructions telling the model to prioritize accuracy above all else and to respond as quickly as possible.
Select the largest available model so capability alone satisfies both accuracy and speed without further measurement.
Launch to a small user group and let subjective feedback decide whether each requirement has been met.

questions.explanation: Both statements become usable once they are **measurable**: a quality target on an agreed evaluation set becomes an eval gate, and a time-to-first-token threshold becomes both an eval criterion and a production monitor. Success criteria should be specific and measurable (the docs' own example is a concrete score on a held-out set), and quality and latency are separate dimensions that each need their own number.

whyWrong.B: Prompt instructions are not requirements: they make nothing enforceable, measurable, or monitorable, and they cannot gate a release.
whyWrong.C: Capability does not substitute for measurement; a larger tier also raises cost and can raise latency, working against one of the two requirements.
whyWrong.D: Subjective beta feedback can supplement quantitative targets, but on its own it cannot gate a release or drive a production monitor.

questions.mindset: If you can't measure it, you can't build, eval, or monitor it.

questions.scenario: A regulated insurer must add a clause-analysis feature. Legal has ruled that policy documents may be processed only inside the company's existing cloud tenancy, which already offers managed Claude access through the cloud provider. The team's cost model favors calling the API directly, and their prototype relied on a direct-API-only capability.
questions.stem: What is the requirements-correct next step?

options.text: Call the direct API anyway and rely on encrypting documents in transit to satisfy the legal ruling.

Treat data residency as a binding constraint: invoke Claude through the cloud provider's managed access inside the tenancy, and verify during design that the models, features, and limits the design depends on are actually available there.
Anonymize the documents upstream, call the direct API with the redacted text, and re-identify the results inside the tenancy.
Ask legal to grant a one-time exception so the team can keep the cheaper direct integration the cost model prefers.

questions.explanation: Data sensitivity and existing cloud contracts are the classic hidden constraints: they are binding, so they decide platform selection ahead of cost preferences. The requirements-correct move is to invoke Claude through the managed access already inside the tenancy — and to verify during design that the needed models, features, and limits exist there, because invoking Claude through third-party platforms is not guaranteed to match the direct API in model availability or capabilities.

whyWrong.A: Encryption in transit does not change where documents are processed and stored, so it does not satisfy a ruling about processing location.
whyWrong.C: Anonymize-and-restore adds a lossy, fragile pipeline — clause analysis depends on exact wording — instead of simply meeting the constraint by processing where the data already lives.
whyWrong.D: Asking legal to bend a binding constraint to preserve a cost preference inverts priority; cost can be optimized inside the constraint, not around it.

questions.mindset: Data-residency and platform constraints outrank cost preferences.

questions.scenario: A SaaS company plans a feature that classifies each inbound support message the moment it arrives and shows the category to the agent taking the case. Projected peak is about 120 requests per minute, each a short prompt. Finance has set a hard ceiling on inference spend per ticket, and support leadership requires the correct category at least 95% of the time on a labeled sample. The team's plan uses the largest model tier, realtime, one call per message.
questions.stem: Which requirement-driven critique should the team act on first?

options.text: Benchmark smaller model tiers against the labeled sample and use the cheapest tier that clears the 95% accuracy floor within the latency budget, instead of defaulting to the largest model.
Switch the per-message classifications to the Message Batches API to halve inference cost, since messages arrive around the clock.
Keep the largest model tier and negotiate the accuracy target upward with support leadership to justify the spend to finance.
Hold each agent's messages and classify them in one combined call per hour to reduce the number of requests.

questions.explanation: The requirement set — short prompts, high volume, a hard spend-per-ticket ceiling, a measurable 95% accuracy floor, and an agent effectively waiting — points at **model tier selection validated by evals**, not a default to the largest model. Benchmarking candidate tiers against the labeled sample and picking the cheapest tier that clears the floor satisfies finance and leadership at once; the alternatives violate either cost or latency requirements.

whyWrong.B: Agents take cases in real time; batch results arrive only when the batch completes (most within an hour, guaranteed within 24 hours), so 'the moment it arrives' fails.
whyWrong.C: Inflating the target to justify spend does not address finance's ceiling, and leadership — not the build team — owns the accuracy requirement.
whyWrong.D: Waiting to classify in hourly groups defeats the show-it-to-the-agent-now requirement; fewer requests do not fix the timing.

questions.mindset: Cost-per-unit plus an accuracy floor means benchmark tiers, don't default to the biggest.

questions.scenario: An internal tool lets analysts ask multiple questions about the same 60-page supplier contract during a working session — typically 10-15 questions spread over an hour. The prototype pasted the full contract text into each new question's user message, and the resulting token invoice alarmed finance.
questions.stem: With minimal change to the product, which data-access design best fits the document reuse and the token budget?

options.text: Have the model produce a one-page summary of the contract at session start and answer later questions from the summary alone.
Send the contract only with the first question and rely on the API to remember it for the rest of the session.
Index the contract in a retrieval store and pass only the top-matching paragraphs with each question.
Keep the contract in the same leading position in every request and mark a cache breakpoint after it, so each follow-up question reuses the cached prefix at a fraction of the input cost.

questions.explanation: Reuse plus size is the classic **prompt caching** case: place the document once in an identical leading position (for example, the first message of the conversation) and mark a cache breakpoint after it, so every follow-up question reads the document from cache at a fraction of base input-token cost instead of re-paying for the full text. The prototype re-sent the whole contract with every question at full price. The API is stateless, so it cannot remember the document across calls; and summaries degrade exactly the precise wording analysts need.

whyWrong.A: Summaries lose precise details first; exact clause wording is exactly what analysts query, so answers would degrade.
whyWrong.B: The Messages API is stateless: each request must carry its own content, so later questions would silently arrive without the contract.
whyWrong.C: Top-paragraph retrieval risks missing clauses whose meaning spans sections, is a larger architectural change than asked for, and is unnecessary while the whole contract fits the context window.

questions.mindset: Reuse plus size means a stable cached prefix, not re-sending the document.

questions.scenario: A team is deciding between realtime Messages API calls and the Message Batches API for a new workload. They list the requirements they have gathered so far.
questions.stem: Which TWO of these findings, if true, point to the Message Batches API rather than realtime calls? Choose TWO.

options.text: Nothing acts on any individual result until the next business day.
An end user is watching the screen and expects an answer within a few seconds.
Each request must run an interactive, multi-step tool-use loop within that same request.
Every response must be JSON that validates against a fixed schema.
Tens of thousands of items must be processed every night and unit cost is the primary constraint.

questions.explanation: Batch fits when no consumer needs an individual result promptly **and** the job is bulk work where unit cost dominates — results then arrive when the batch completes (most finish within an hour, guaranteed within 24 hours) at roughly half the token cost. A waiting user or an interactive multi-step tool loop requires realtime; JSON output works in both modes and does not discriminate.

whyWrong.B: A user waiting seconds needs realtime; batch completion is asynchronous and only guaranteed within a 24-hour window.
whyWrong.C: Batch requests cannot stream and cannot run interactive multi-turn tool loops inside a single request; agentic loops need realtime calls.
whyWrong.D: Both modes can return schema-validated structured output, so JSON alone does not select the mode.

questions.mindset: Batch fits latency-tolerant bulk work; humans and interactive tool loops need realtime.

questions.scenario: A team is drafting the requirements document for a production Claude feature before any design work begins. Reviewers are rejecting statements that cannot be tested or observed.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements are usable requirements as written, because each is measurable and can gate an eval or a production monitor? Choose TWO.

options.text: The system should always use the most capable model available so quality is never compromised.
At least 95% of extracted fields must exactly match gold labels on the agreed 500-document benchmark before release.
Responses should be helpful and written in a tone that fits the brand.
Median time to first token must stay under 2 seconds and the 95th percentile under 5 seconds at projected peak load.
The model must never make a mistake or hallucinate once the feature is in production.

questions.explanation: A requirement is usable when it is **measurable**, so it can gate an eval or drive a monitor: a field-accuracy threshold on an agreed benchmark and a time-to-first-token budget at peak load both qualify. The docs model this directly — success criteria like a concrete score on a held-out set, and latency measured as time-to-first-token — and note that success criteria are usually multi-dimensional (quality and latency measured separately).

whyWrong.A: This names a solution (model choice) rather than a system property, and 'most capable' is neither measurable nor bounded by cost.
whyWrong.C: Helpfulness and tone are legitimate eval categories, but as written the statement has no scale or rubric, so it cannot gate anything.
whyWrong.E: Perfect output is unachievable and therefore unactionable; requirements must bound acceptable error rates on an agreed test set.

questions.mindset: Requirements must be measurable to gate releases and drive monitors.

questions.scenario: A live assistant drafts long email replies for support agents. It works, but agents stare at a blank screen for the better part of a minute before the finished draft appears all at once. Output quality is fine; leadership wants the wait to feel shorter without changing what is produced and without materially increasing spend.
questions.stem: What is the best fit for this requirement?

options.text: Switch to a smaller model tier so drafts are produced faster.
Move drafting to the Message Batches API and deliver drafts to agents when they are ready.
Keep the realtime integration and enable streaming, so agents see the draft begin almost immediately as it is generated.
Shorten drafts with an aggressive word-count cap so there is less text to generate.

questions.explanation: The requirement is **perceived responsiveness** with unchanged output and cost: streaming delivers exactly that, because time to first token drops as soon as generation begins, while token cost and content stay the same. Model swaps and length caps change what is produced; batching makes the wait dramatically worse for someone watching the screen.

whyWrong.A: Swapping tiers can change what is drafted — leadership asked for the same output — and raw generation speed is not the same as perceived responsiveness.
whyWrong.B: Batching makes interactive waiting worse, not better: drafts would arrive within a window of up to 24 hours.
whyWrong.D: An aggressive word cap changes the product output; it addresses length, not the blank-screen wait.

questions.mindset: Streaming fixes perceived latency without changing output or cost.

questions.scenario: A company has approved three Claude workloads: (1) an in-call assistant that whispers answers to support agents live; (2) a nightly compliance sweep that scores all 80,000 of the day's transcripts; (3) a quarterly board report written from a small set of long strategy documents where quality clearly outranks cost. A lead engineer proposes standardizing all three on one pattern — the largest model, realtime calls through a single shared agent service — "to keep the architecture simple."
questions.stem: What is the best requirements-driven response?

options.text: Standardize all three workloads on the Message Batches API instead, since two of the three are not latency-sensitive.

Match each workload to its own pattern — streaming realtime for the in-call assistant, the Batches API for the nightly sweep, a capable model for the quarterly report — sharing only cross-cutting infrastructure such as logging and secrets management.
Adopt the shared agent service for all three but configure per-workload model IDs, keeping every call realtime.
Accept the single-pattern proposal now and revisit the nightly sweep's cost only if the invoice becomes a problem.

questions.explanation: The three workloads have different latency tolerances, volumes, and quality bars, so each should get the pattern its requirements dictate: streaming realtime for the human-waiting assistant, the Batches API for the latency-tolerant bulk sweep, and a capable model for the low-volume, quality-first report. Standardizing on any single pattern breaks at least one workload. Share logging and secrets — not the integration pattern.

whyWrong.A: Forcing batch onto the live assistant breaks its latency requirement — the mirror image of the proposed mistake.
whyWrong.C: Per-workload model IDs fix the tier but leave the nightly sweep on full-price realtime calls and shoehorn a batch job into an always-on agent service.
whyWrong.D: Deferring a known, quantified cost mismatch postpones a decision the requirements already support: latency-tolerant bulk work belongs in batches.

questions.mindset: Match each workload to its own pattern; share infrastructure, not the pattern.

questions.scenario: A product sponsor's kickoff brief for a Claude feature lists everything the model might someday do: triage inbound tickets, draft replies, translate replies into four languages, detect refund fraud, and write a monthly trend report. The sponsor asks the team to commit to building all of it in one release "so the platform is settled once."
questions.stem: Following requirements-driven design, what should the team recommend to minimize delivery risk while keeping the platform open to the full vision?

options.text: Ship the core ticket-triage flow first against measurable acceptance criteria, then add capabilities one by one as production results justify the added complexity.
Commit to the full list in one release; because Claude is general-purpose, one agent can absorb every capability without added risk.
Build all five capabilities now, but as five separate agents behind a shared router, so each one stays simple.
Decline the four additional capabilities permanently and record them as out of scope for the platform.

questions.explanation: The sponsor's list is a wish list, not a validated requirement set. Requirements-driven design delivers the smallest scope that meets a **measurable acceptance criterion**, instruments it in production, and adds capability only when results justify the complexity — the "start simple, add complexity only when it demonstrably helps" principle. Committing to all five capabilities at once maximizes cost, latency, and compounding failure modes before any value is proven.

whyWrong.B: General-purpose does not mean risk-free: each capability adds cost, latency, eval surface, and failure modes, and one monolithic release delays all learning until everything works.
whyWrong.C: A router plus five agents adds orchestration infrastructure and operational surface before any capability has proven value; complexity must be justified by demonstrated need, not pre-built.
whyWrong.D: Deferral pending evidence is not refusal; requirements should evolve with production results, and permanently recording legitimate future needs out of scope discards them.

questions.mindset: Start simple; add complexity only when it demonstrably helps.

questions.scenario: A store-chain assistant answers questions such as "how many units of item X are left at the Y branch?" Inventory changes constantly. The current design pastes a full inventory export into the system prompt each morning, and by afternoon the answers are wrong.
questions.stem: Which requirement-driven fix best addresses the failure?

options.text: Regenerate the inventory export every 30 minutes and paste the larger snapshot into the prompt.
Instruct the model to preface every stock answer with "as of this morning's data" so agents know its limits.
Move to a model with a larger context window so the complete inventory always fits in the prompt.
Make freshness the deciding requirement: give the assistant a tool that queries the live inventory service at question time, instead of embedding a snapshot in the prompt.

questions.explanation: Freshness is the deciding **data-access requirement**: data access patterns (inline, files, tools, retrieval) are chosen by size, freshness, reuse, and sensitivity — and only a tool that queries the inventory service at question time yields current answers. Snapshots pasted into the prompt are stale the moment they land, waste context, and scale poorly with catalog size.

whyWrong.A: Faster snapshots are still stale between refreshes, bloat the prompt, and get worse as the inventory grows.
whyWrong.B: Announcing staleness documents the defect rather than fixing it; agents asked for current stock, not a disclaimer.
whyWrong.C: Context capacity is not the problem — the data's age is; a bigger window just holds more stale numbers.

questions.mindset: Freshness decides the data-access pattern: live tools beat stale snapshots.

questions.scenario: During requirements gathering for a Claude-powered claims feature, the team collects statements from stakeholders. Some are hard constraints that narrow the solution architecture; others are preferences that design can trade off.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements are binding constraints that should shape the architecture before detailed design begins? Choose TWO.

options.text: The UX team prefers claim summaries to open with a friendly one-line recap.
The engineers would rather implement the service in TypeScript than in Python.
Claim text may not be sent to any endpoint outside the company's approved cloud region.
Product would like summary quality to keep improving each quarter as long as budget allows.
The feature must be live before the manual-review vendor contract renews in six weeks.

questions.explanation: Binding constraints narrow the architecture before design: **where data may be processed** dictates platform selection, and a **fixed delivery deadline** caps solution complexity and scope. These are exactly the hidden constraints — data sensitivity, existing contracts, and time — that decide the correct architecture. Preferences such as tone, implementation language, and open-ended quality aspirations live in the trade-space design can negotiate.

whyWrong.A: A presentation preference sits in the design trade-space; nothing architectural is fixed by it.
whyWrong.B: As stated this is a preference ('would rather'), not a mandate; both languages are viable for Claude integrations.
whyWrong.D: An unbounded aspiration with no measurable bar or committed budget cannot constrain the architecture.

questions.mindset: Constraints bind the architecture; preferences are trade-space.

questions.scenario: During discovery for a Claude invoice-processing feature, a business analyst captures a mix of requirement statements. Some describe what the system must do; others describe how well it must perform while doing it.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements are non-functional requirements that should constrain infrastructure and model selection? Choose TWO.

options.text: The system must extract the vendor name, invoice number, and line-item totals from each invoice.
The system must sustain at least 4,000 invoices per hour during month-end peak.
Invoices that look like duplicates must be flagged for human review before posting.
At least 98% of extracted amounts must match gold labels on the agreed 500-invoice benchmark before release.
The extraction prompt and output schema must be version-controlled alongside the service code.

questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements describe **how well** the system must operate — throughput, accuracy, latency, cost — and those are what constrain model tier, API mode, and infrastructure. A throughput floor (4,000 invoices per hour at peak) and an accuracy floor (98% on an agreed benchmark) both qualify, and both double as eval gates and production monitors, which is exactly how measurable success criteria are meant to be reused.

whyWrong.A: Describes a function — what the system does — not how well it must do it.
whyWrong.C: Also functional: it defines behavior (flag duplicates for review), not a quality target.
whyWrong.E: Good engineering practice, but a process control rather than a measurable operating property of the running system.

questions.mindset: Non-functional requirements (throughput, accuracy, latency, cost) drive infrastructure choices.
